PassphraseVerifier-151-boolean-1.why: Skipping empty fields would read `<valid>$`, `$<valid>` or `…$$…` as a four-field verifier. Killed by "a stored value with an empty fifth field is malformed…" (002781d).

PassphraseVerifier-189-boolean-11.why: The catch path in `matches` was unreached: no scheme in the tests throws from `derive`. A test scheme that always throws now must match nothing (002781d).

PassphraseVerifier-205-logical-17.why: `PassphraseVerifier.==` had no test at all in these suites. Killed by "two verifiers are equal exactly when every stored field is" (002781d), which varies one field at a time.

PassphraseScheme-30-boolean-0.why: The protocol's default `isBelowCurrentCost` (never) was untested; every scheme in the tests overrode it or wasn't asked. Killed by "a scheme that declares no cost policy is never below its current cost" (002781d).

PassphraseScheme-56-constant-4.why: `Int(parameters) ?? 0` vs `?? 1`: the fallback is reached only for parameters that aren't an integer, and both 0 and 1 are below `defaultRounds`, so the answer (true) is the same. Such parameters can't reach a constructed verifier anyway: `isValid` rejects them on decode and on derive.

PassphraseScheme-82-boolean-6.why: Legacy's `isBelowCurrentCost` was only exercised where the identifier differed from the writing scheme's, which already forces an upgrade. Now tested directly and with legacy as the writing scheme (002781d).

PassphraseScheme-97-constant-11.why: Asking PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 for 33 bytes: its first 32 are the 32-byte output (block T1 is identical), and the copy loop keeps only `derived.count` = 32 of them. Confirmed with Python's hashlib: the 33-byte output is the 32-byte one plus `06`.

PassphraseScheme-104-constant-12.why: The buffer's fill value: every one of its 32 bytes is overwritten by the 32-byte key before it is returned.

PassphraseScheme-104-constant-13.why: A 33-byte digest (the 32-byte key plus a zero) would still self-verify. Killed by the PBKDF2 known-answer test, whose vector comes from Python's hashlib (002781d).

PassphraseScheme-106-relational-14.why: `offset < derived.count` vs `<=`: the key's buffer is 32 bytes, so `offset` never exceeds 31 and the bound is never the deciding test.

PassphraseScheme-136-deletion-17.why: "`writing` is accepted too, whether or not it's listed" was untested: every test listed it. Killed by "the writing scheme is accepted even when the list leaves it out" and the tests built on `PassphraseSchemes([], writing:)` (002781d).

Authenticator-78-relational-1.why: Not equivalent, though it looks like it. With one credential, `disableTogether` can only change a key whose count is at the ceiling but whose flag isn't set: a last admitted attempt still being checked by another request. The mutant flags it, and that attempt's success can then no longer clear it (P22). Killed by "P22: a lone credential turned away doesn't seal the in-flight last attempt's fate" (6c0411e).

ThrottleLedger-58-constant-1.why: The salt-length prefix's high byte, `count >> 8` vs `>> 9`: both are 0 for any salt under 256 bytes, and this package writes 16-byte salts. A stored salt of 256+ bytes would get a different, still deterministic and still per-salt key: no throttling property depends on the exact fingerprint.

ThrottleLedger-59-deletion-3.why: Without hashing the salt, every passphrase with a 16-byte salt got the same key, so rebinding inherited the old count. Killed by "a new passphrase is a new key…" (8b7b788).

ThrottleLedger-85-negation-5.why: `ThrottleKey.oneTimeCode` wasn't tested directly in these suites. Killed by "an enrolled app's key is the subject's own…" (8b7b788).

ThrottleLedger-89-deletion-8.why: Same as the passphrase key: without hashing the sealed bytes, a re-enrolled app inherited the old key. Killed by the same test (8b7b788).

ThrottleLedger-131-relational-14.why: The backoff's end instant was untested. Killed by "a backoff refuses until the instant it ends, and not at that instant" (8b7b788).

ThrottleLedger-304-relational-30.why: `LedgerBook.maximumEntries` had no test at all. Killed by "a full book refuses an attempt on a new key, and admits one below the limit" (8b7b788).

ThrottleLedger-311-relational-36.why: The comment's "at the ceiling, no backoff" was untested. Killed by "P13: the attempt that reaches the ceiling earns no backoff" (8b7b788).

ThrottleLedger-324-arithmetic-43.why: The limit on a multi-key failure. Killed by "a failure involving new keys is refused if adding them all would pass the limit" (8b7b788).

ThrottleLedger-359-early-return-69.why: `changed` is what decides whether the file ledger writes; a success with nothing to clear reported a change. Killed by "a success with nothing to clear changes nothing…" (8b7b788).

ThrottleLedger-374-boolean-82.why: Same: disabling keys already disabled reported a change, a needless write. Killed by "disabling keys that are all disabled already changes nothing" (8b7b788).

ThrottleLedger-375-boolean-84.why: A real hole in coverage: the mutant skipped keys the ledger already held (enabled, with failures) and disabled only new ones. Killed by "P13: disabling together reaches a key the ledger already has" (8b7b788).

FileThrottleLedger-175-constant-12.why: `open` returning descriptor 0 needs stdin closed; it's open in every process this runs in, so `>= 0` and `>= 1` decide alike. (In a daemon that closed stdin, the mutant would refuse a good lock file; the original is correct.)

FileThrottleLedger-186-relational-19.class: Untestable without fault injection — accepted, explained
FileThrottleLedger-186-relational-19.why: The `EINTR` retry bound on `flock`. Reaching it needs a signal delivered without `SA_RESTART` while `flock` blocks, a hundred times over; no test can arrange that in-process without a seam in the source.

FileThrottleLedger-189-arithmetic-20.class: Untestable without fault injection — accepted, explained
FileThrottleLedger-189-arithmetic-20.why: The same `EINTR` path: the counter only advances after an interrupted `flock`.

FileThrottleLedger-229-arithmetic-33.why: Reading `maximumBytes - 1` truncated a valid ledger at exactly the limit. Killed by "a ledger of exactly the size limit is read whole; one byte over is refused" (8b7b788).

FileThrottleLedger-229-constant-34.why: Reading up to `maximumBytes + 2` rather than `+ 1`: any file over the limit still yields more than `maximumBytes` bytes and is refused; any file within it is read whole either way.

FileThrottleLedger-262-relational-40.why: Rows sorted descending instead of ascending. The documented property is "the same state is always the same bytes", which either order gives; nothing reads the order.

FileThrottleLedger-281-boolean-46.class: Untestable without fault injection — accepted, explained
FileThrottleLedger-281-boolean-46.why: `renamed` starting true would leak the temporary file when writing or renaming fails after it was created. Only an I/O failure in that window (ENOSPC, EIO, a failed `rename`) reaches it, and every route to one a test controls fails earlier, at `open` or at `readBook`. Closing it needs a fault-injection seam in `writeBook`.

FileThrottleLedger-282-negation-47.why: Inverting the cleanup unlinks the temporary after a successful rename, when that name no longer exists (ENOENT, nothing removed), and skips it on failure, which is mutant 281's untestable window.

FileThrottleLedger-290-deletion-50.class: Untestable without fault injection — accepted, explained
FileThrottleLedger-290-deletion-50.why: Dropping `synchronize()` loses durability across a crash or power loss, which no in-process test observes: the page cache serves the same bytes.

FileThrottleLedger-296-boolean-53.why: As 282: after a successful rename, unlinking the temporary's old name removes nothing.

Argon2id-364-constant-171.why: `addressInput[1] = pass` instead of `[0]` (then overwritten by `lane`), leaving `[0]` at its reset 0. Argon2id uses data-independent addressing only in pass 0 (slices 0 and 1), so `pass` is always 0 when the address block is built: the block is identical.

BLAKE2b-113-relational-285.why: `offset < end` vs `<=`: when they're equal the loop `offset..<end` is empty and the zeroed words are returned either way.

OneTimeCode-61-boolean-2.why: Skipping empty fields in `totp-…` can change what `split` returns, but the initializer then requires `self.identifier == identifier`, and a canonical identifier has no empty field, so every input the mutant would newly parse is still refused.

OneTimeCode-73-logical-11.why: No test had exactly one of digits and step out of range. Killed by "parameters are valid only when both the digits and the step are" (40f6c3d).

OneTimeCode-80-constant-14.why: The SHA-512 key length was untested (SHA-1 and SHA-256 were). Killed by "an SHA-512 key is the hash's output length: 512 bits" (40f6c3d).

OneTimeCode-104-arithmetic-26.why: `offset + 3 < mac.count`: `offset` is `last & 0x0F` ≤ 15 and the shortest HMAC is 20 bytes, so the guard always passes; `offset - 3` passes too.

OneTimeCode-182-boolean-42.why: A stored verifier with a stray `$` was accepted. Killed by "a stored value with a stray separator is malformed" (40f6c3d).

OneTimeCode-251-boolean-58.why: Only SHA-1 enrollment was tested, and a 20-byte key needs no Base32 padding. Killed by "the enrollment secret is unpadded Base32…" with a 32-byte key (40f6c3d).

PassphrasePolicy-151-relational-9.why: The byte cap's boundary was untested. Killed by "exactly 1 KiB is looked at…" (40f6c3d).

PassphrasePolicy-330-boolean-23.why: `ContextWords.contains(_:)` (no context) was never called. Killed by "context words, asked without a context, contain nothing" (40f6c3d).

PassphrasePolicy-362-boolean-33.why: The default argument of `PassphraseGuidance.init`'s `requiresLettersAndDigits`: its one caller, `PassphrasePolicy.guidance`, always passes it explicitly.

PassphrasePolicy-374-constant-34.why: Where the PCI line goes in the guidance was unpinned. Killed by "the PCI profile's composition rule comes straight after the length rule" (40f6c3d).
